content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper introduces two losses, dscl (decoupled supervised contrastive los) and pbsd (patch-based self distillation), to address long-tail image recognition tasks. Observing the fact that supervised contrastive loss can be influenced by the imbalanced dataset, this paper investigated how to adapt supervised contrastive learning to long-tail recognition and proposed a decoupled supervised contrastive learning loss. Specifically, a new definition of positive and negative views for head/tail classes can reduce the influence of imbalanced training and lead to performance gain. A patch-based self-distillation loss is also introduced to leverage the power of small patches.

The experiments are very solid, clearly demonstrating the superiority of the proposed methods. Multiple baselines are compared in two datasets with varying settings. The ablation study is also solid.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths: 

1: The key observation regarding supervised contrastive loss is insightful, thus this paper is well-motivated.

2: Very solid experiments and ablation study. 

3: Good performance. The proposed method surpasses previous SOTA by large margins. 

Weaknesses:

1: The main contribution is somehow a little bit unclear. From the ablation study, we can see the performance gain is mostly from PBSD. However this paper is mostly motivated by supervised contrastive learning, that is, the DSCL part.  Other than improving the discriminative of the learned representation on tail classes, any other motivations for PBSD?

2: No experiments regarding smaller-size datasets (CIFAR). Both ImageNet and iNaturaList contain relatively large images. It is necessary to validate whether the proposed method, especially the PBSD part can scale to small-size images (let's say, 32*32 resolution).  It would be very interesting to add an study regarding image resolution (some candidates: 32, 64, 128, 224, 384).

Minor issues:

1: Fig 1 can be modified. The size of the clouds is not identical.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: Good clarity.

Quality: Good paper. The quality meets the acceptance bar. 

Novelty: Not very novel. Incremental on supervised contrastive learning and part-based methods.

Reproducibility: Training details are provided. Authors claimed code release.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall I'm leaning to accept. If authors can address my concerns listed in weaknesses, I will consider further rising my rating to accept.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposed two methods to improve the supervised constrastive learning under long tail distribution: decoupled supervised contrastive loss (DSCL) and patch-based self distillation (PBSD). DSCL separates the supervised contrastive loss to semantic and appearance features to aviod difference on the weights caused by different cardinalities. PBSD proposes to utilize small patches for supervised contrastive learning.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Pros:

1. The performance improvements seem encouraging

2. The two proposed methods are clearly explained in Figure 1.

Cons:

1. Lack of novelty. DSCL sounds like a trick of adjusting the hyperparameters. PBSD cannot be treated as a contribution, given it is known as the multi-crop trick and has been employed in a lot of methods (e.g. swav[1], DINO[2], iBot[3])

	[1] Caron, Mathilde, et al. "Unsupervised learning of visual features by contrasting cluster assignments." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 33 (2020): 9912-9924.

	[2] Caron, M., Touvron, H., Misra, I., Jégou, H., Mairal, J., Bojanowski, P., & Joulin, A. (2021). Emerging properties in self-supervised vision transformers. In Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF International Conference on Computer Vision (pp. 9650-9660).

	[3] Zhou, Jinghao, et al. "ibot: Image bert pre-training with online tokenizer." arXiv preprint arXiv:2111.07832 (2021).

3. Many studies of contrastive learning under long tail distribution are ignored. For example [4][5][6][7][8]

	[4] Yang, Yuzhe, and Zhi Xu. "Rethinking the value of labels for improving class-imbalanced learning." Advances in neural information processing systems 33 (2020): 19290-19301.

	[5] Jiang, Ziyu, et al. "Self-damaging contrastive learning." International Conference on Machine Learning. PMLR, 2021.

	[6] Wang, Peng, et al. "Contrastive learning based hybrid networks for long-tailed image classification." Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF conference on computer vision and pattern recognition. 2021.

	[7] Jiang, Ziyu, et al. "Improving contrastive learning on imbalanced data via open-world sampling." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 34 (2021): 5997-6009.

	[8] Zhou, Zhihan, et al. "Contrastive Learning with Boosted Memorization." International Conference on Machine Learning. PMLR, 2022.

4. Misuse of cite and citep. The cite in many places should be replaced by citep.

5. The layout of the method part is a little weird (e.g. too long overview).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: Good. 

Quality: Fair. (requires further improvement as discussed in Cons)

Novelty: Limited. (as discussed in Cons)

Reproducibility: Good. I think it can be reproduced given authors promise the code release.

2. The result seems good, which is competitive among the recent works.


Weakness

For the decoupled supervised contrastive loss, the authors claim that “target distribution is not suitable to the long-tailed recognition task, as it can lead to the biased model” and the strategy to tackle the problem is to fix the weight of positive sample from augmentation. I don’t understand why the mean of contrastive loss leads to biased model and how the fixed weight addresses it.

2. The recent works compared with in Table 2 are mostly trained only with supervised loss and 90 epochs. However, the work is trained with supervised contrastive loss and 200 epochs. It would be better to provide more fair comparison results of latest contrastive loss based methods.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes patch-based contrastive learning for long-tailed recognition. The authors propose to extract patches from different data augmentations of the same image, and add a contrastive loss term, which considers the patch similarity between the patches extracted from the same image, as well as other images from the same class. The authors also propose a hyperparameter alpha, which balances the target dataset distribution. The experiments are only conducted in two datasets, ImageNet-LT and iNaturalist18.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The proposed method appears to achieve a good performance in ImageNet-LT.

Weaknesses:
- The paper presentation is not clear, see "Clarity, Quality, Novelty And Reproducibility" for more details.
- The authors re-design the target distribution, so that the class priors are balanced. How is that different from balanced sampling in (Kang et al. 2019) or logit adjustment (Menon et al. 2020)?
- How does q(t,s j i ) compute the relationship of shared patterns between different classes? Doesn't t still come from the ground-truth of the training set, and therefore enforce similarity of patches from the same class?
- Only two datasets (ImageNet-LT, iNaturalist-18) are used for experiments. Experiments in another dataset (Places365-LT or iNaturalist17) would have helped.
- When alpha=0, the difference in accuracy is only 0.9 compared to the optimal alpha. This is not a significant difference. Did the authors repeat this experiment many times with different random seeds? If yes, what is the variance of this difference?
- Figure 3 (Left) contains a dotted green line (supervised contrastive loss), which again is not much different from using alpha.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The presentation and the writing in this paper is not clear. Some examples:

- \hat{p}_{dscl} and q_{pbsd} are introduced in Equations 5 and 6, respectively, but not defined until Equations 8 and 9. This makes it hard for the reader to follow the presentation.
- Citations follow the wrong format, e.g. TSC Li et al. (2021b) should be TSC(Li et al. 2021b)
- Experiments are not clear, e.g. it's not state which dataset is used for the experiments in Figure 3?
- Why does Figure 3 (Middle) contain a blue line?
- The best performing numbers should be bolded on Table 2. For example, the proposed method is behind SOTA in iNaturalist18.
content.summary_of_the_review: The presentation is not clear, and some of the claims in the paper, such as why alpha is useful, or how common visual patterns are learned between different classes are not well supported. The experiments are also not clear, and fail to verify the claims made in the paper. Therefore, my initial rating is reject.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper addressed the problem of long-tail recognition and provides a solution based on a new kind of contrastive loss. Even though the technical details are not described clear enough the experimental results indicate the benefits of the approach.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

The paper addressed an important task and shows that the proposed approach finally yields better results


Weaknesses:

On the downside, however, the quality of presentation is insufficient. In this way, the motivation for the approach is not clear at all, and the technical writing does not allow it all to follow the details.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
In general, the approach seems to be novel, however, neither the motivation nor the technical details are clear enough.  In this way, the quality and clarity of the paper needs to be improved. There is not reading and argumentation flow and many aspects are not fully clear. The most important points are given below:

The caption of Fig. 1 does not cover the presented information at all. Thus, for a better understanding, this must be adjusted. In its current form the figure does not help to comprehend the problem. The same also applies for Fig.2.

From the introduction the motivation for the proposed loss is not fully clear. In particular, at this point the benefits compared to related approaches are not clear at all.

In the related works section, many references are given, but the single approaches are not discussed at all. Thus, similar to the introduction, the expected benefits from the presented contribution is not clear at all.

The mathematical writing must be seriously checked, in particular how to correct embed the equations into the text. Since this is done in an inconsistent wrong way, reading the technical part is hampered!

The formulation in Eq.(1) is more general not limited to long-tailed classification problems. Moreover, reformulate the equation to a correct mathematical formulation.

Starting from Eq.(2), Sec.3.1 is  hard to follow. There is no argumentation flow, used notation is often not introduced (sufficiently), and it is not clear at all where just prior work is described and where a new contribution is discussed.

The advantage of the the loss function defined in Eq.(7) is not clear at all. Moreover, the importance of the weight parameter is not clear at this point.

Sec.3.2 and 3.3 are written a little bit chattily and is not focused at all. 

It is not clear if the results in Fig.3 have been obtained from the experiment on ImageNet-LT?

The results presented in Fig.4 are not fully clear.

Use the correct citation style for "NeurIPS".

Check the paper titles in the bibliography for correctness.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper's topic is important and the results indicate benefits compared to existing approaches. However, there are too many flaws hampering the paper in its current form.
